name: openclaw
notes: openclaw/openclaw, TypeScript. Its Gateway is the local control plane for sessions, tools, events and channel connections, so it does hold sessions behind a daemon.

Pinned to npm `openclaw@2026.7.1-2`, which matches GitHub release v2026.7.1-2 and is the `latest` dist-tag at 2026-08-28. Identity checked before installing: the package is published by maintainer `steipete` with `repository: git+https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw.git`. The impersonating package `@openclaw-ai/openclawai`, which steals credentials and installs a RAT, was never fetched.

LICENCE, resolved: MIT. The GitHub API reports NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file at this tag is the verbatim MIT text plus a closing sentence pointing at THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, which defeats GitHub's classifier; package.json declares "license": "MIT". A comparison that names a licence should name MIT.

Like zeroclaw it is documented as designed for a single operator running locally, not a multi-user server. Throughput and the per-session memory ramp are therefore not declared: they would measure a design goal the project does not have.
Node, so the fixed memory floor is large. Only a slope or a delta says anything about per-session cost here, never an absolute footprint.

Two surfaces on one port, because neither answers all three probes alone: the control-plane WebSocket carries `sessions.create` and `sessions.delete`, which have no HTTP route, and `POST /v1/chat/completions` carries the turns. The docs say a request through the latter 'runs as a normal Gateway agent run (same codepath as `openclaw agent`)'; `model` is an agent target and `x-openclaw-session-key` routes the turn into a session this benchmark already created, so a turn number is a turn in an existing session rather than an implicit create folded into the first message.
Config differences from a stock install are listed at the top of launch.sh: auth off on loopback, the chat-completions endpoint enabled, and the scripted provider.

Session routing was verified, not assumed: three turns sent with one `x-openclaw-session-key` reached the model as 2, then 4, then 6 messages, and `GET /sessions/{key}/history` returned a single transcript with all six. The header is honoured, so a turn number here is a turn in an existing session.

Which means the turn numbers rise with session length, and visibly: over the 200 turns of one probe, round_trip ran from 996 ms at the start to 1578 ms at the end. The p50 is the middle of that, not a first-turn cost. Every session-kernel subject is driven the same way — one session, many turns — so the method is comparable, but OpenClaw's slope is steep enough that its p50 must be quoted with the turn count beside it.
The runner's fixture count came out at exactly one model call per turn, so nothing was answered from a cache or a replay path.

create.definition: `sessions.create` on the Gateway control plane until it returns the session key — the same call the Control UI's new-session button makes. The control connection is opened in `prepare` and is not inside this number

ttfb.definition: `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `stream: true` submitted until the first non-empty assistant content delta; scripted provider via a `models.providers` entry

round_trip.definition: `POST /v1/chat/completions` submitted until the response carrying the completed assistant message
